components.title: The Water Cycle
components.subtitle: Understanding how water moves through Earth's atmosphere, land, and oceans

components.title: What You'll Learn
components.description: Explore the continuous movement of water through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation—the three key processes that drive our planet's water cycle.

blocks.label: FOUNDATION
blocks.title: What is the Water Cycle?
blocks.body:
The water cycle is the continuous movement of water on, above, and below Earth's surface. Water changes between three states—solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (water vapor)—as it moves through different parts of our environment.

This cycle is powered by the sun's energy and gravity, and it's essential for all life on Earth.

blocks.label: INTERMEDIATE
blocks.title: The Three Main Processes
blocks.body:
**Evaporation**: Water from oceans, lakes, and rivers turns into water vapor when heated by the sun. This vapor rises into the atmosphere.

**Condensation**: As water vapor rises and cools in the upper atmosphere, it transforms back into liquid water droplets, forming clouds.

**Precipitation**: When water droplets in clouds become heavy enough, they fall back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
blocks.takeaway: Sun's heat → Evaporation → Condensation → Precipitation → Repeat

blocks.label: ADVANCED
blocks.title: Transpiration and Groundwater Flow
blocks.body:
**Transpiration**: Plants absorb water through their roots and release water vapor through their leaves. This process, combined with evaporation, is called evapotranspiration.

**Groundwater Flow**: Some precipitation infiltrates the soil and becomes groundwater, which slowly moves through rock layers and can feed springs, rivers, and aquifers. This water may take years or centuries to return to the surface.
blocks.code:
Evapotranspiration = Evaporation + Transpiration
Groundwater residence time: months to millennia
blocks.code_caption: Key formulas and timescales in the water cycle

blocks.label: WORKED EXAMPLE
blocks.title: Tracing a Water Molecule's Journey
blocks.body:
Imagine a water molecule in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii:

1. **Day 1**: The sun heats the ocean surface. Our molecule evaporates and becomes water vapor, rising into the atmosphere.

2. **Days 2-3**: The vapor drifts eastward with trade winds, cooling as it rises. It condenses into a cloud droplet over the central Pacific.

3. **Day 4**: The cloud grows heavy with millions of droplets. Our molecule falls as rain on the Big Island of Hawaii.

4. **Days 5-10**: The rainwater soaks into volcanic soil, becoming groundwater that slowly percolates through rock layers.

5. **Months later**: The groundwater emerges in a spring, flows into a stream, and eventually returns to the ocean.

The entire journey might take 6-12 months—but some groundwater can remain underground for thousands of years!
blocks.takeaway: Water molecules continuously cycle through the environment at different timescales

components.title: Key Takeaways
components.text:
• The water cycle is driven by solar energy and gravity
• Water continuously changes states: solid ↔ liquid ↔ gas
• Evaporation, condensation, and precipitation are the primary processes
• Transpiration and groundwater flow extend the cycle's complexity
• Different water molecules take different paths and timescales

questions.question: Which process describes water vapor turning into liquid water droplets in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Condensation is the process where water vapor cools and transforms into liquid water droplets, forming clouds. Evaporation is the reverse process, precipitation is water falling, and transpiration is water released by plants.

questions.question: What is the primary energy source that powers the water cycle?
questions.explanation: The sun's heat energy drives evaporation and atmospheric circulation. While gravity helps water fall as precipitation and flow downhill, the sun is the primary energy source for the entire cycle.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a direct part of the water cycle?
questions.explanation: While photosynthesis uses water, it is not a direct part of the water cycle itself. Evaporation, condensation, and precipitation are the core processes. Transpiration (water released by plants) is part of the cycle, but photosynthesis is not.

on_pass.title: Great Work!
on_pass.description: You've demonstrated a solid understanding of the water cycle. You're ready to explore more advanced topics like climate patterns and water conservation.

on_fail.title: Review Needed
on_fail.description: Take another look at the concept sections above, especially the intermediate and advanced levels. Pay close attention to the definitions of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
